posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
A game design document is like writing an outline for an essay.
It's helpful if you're the kind of person it's helpful to.
And whether it's "quality" or not is going to be dependent on whether it contains the information you find personally useful in guiding your work.
That said, I Googled "rpg game design document" and got pages of results, so there are surely things you can find useful.
And I really don't understand the first part where you're making a project to help other people finish projects.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I'm not sure what you're asking for.
By and large, a "game design document" is an internal document to organize your project.  Which means, it's going to change from person to person, and what's useful for one isn't going to be useful for another.
The easiest way to think of them is as an outline of your "High Concept" that is your game.
If you don't know what "High Concept" is, I suggest you google it.
Heck, the only stuff I keep in my own Game Design Document are:
1.  The "10 Plot Points" for my story.
2.  Characters and classes.
3.  Items and Weapon concepts.
4.  Themes of the game.
5.  Basic outline and purpose of each system in use.
It's like... 4 pages and a short Excel document.  I refer back to it whenever I'm going to make a change.  That's it.
Having a GDD doesn't, in any way, guarantee someone will finish their game.  But, having one can usually prevent "scope creep".

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
Mr_Chickenwing said:
Here is a fantastic template with a lot of questions for you to answer.
Click to expand...
It's probably worth a quick mention that that form is clearly intended for people making educational games for a class.
Anyone reading it ought to be able to adapt it to the purpose of a hobby or commercial game, but there are a few questions that one ought not try to answer as asked because they don't apply.
For example, the vast majority of people here won't have a pedagogical objective or social impact for their game - I would probably skip that entire game overview section, as what I would put in there (mechanics and story) are addressed separately later. I think the only pertinent bit in there is genre.

posts.author: alasth
posts.body:
Personally, I use a discord server and google sheet to manage my project collaboratively :
- Discord allows me to invite people to help me, and test my project, with channels for each subject, so as not to mix everything up.
- Google Sheet is my true Game design document with lots of things: (I must have more than twenty sheets
)
I often work away from home, where I don't have access to RPG Maker, but where I log the whole database: objects, monsters, etc. and also the whole formula part.
I like to create my own battle formulas (bye bye a.att - b.def) and sheet allows me to create a simulator with all the formulas integrated.
Once I'm in and running RMMV, I can copy/paste everything I've built externally without having to access RM.

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
It's hard to give a single design doc template "for RPGs" because even within that genre, there are so many variables. Are you making a sprawling 60-hour epic, or a compact 1-hour adventure? Are you working with a team, or working solo? Are you the kind of person who likes to have a super-detailed outline of your stories before you start writing, or are you the kind of person that finds writing a super-detailed outline sucks the fun out of writing the actual story? All of those things will affect what your design doc will look like and how it will be used.
Personally, I don't have a template for my design docs--I write them for each project. But some things that I always end up including are the "vibe," the audience, the very general plot progression, the main mechanics/gimmicks,  and the list of important places and people. Also, the credits list! This is hugely important, and the design doc is a very convenient place to keep track of it.
If your design doc is going to be used by a team, it will need to be more detailed than a design doc intended only for you. A design doc for a team should include which team members are responsible for which things, as well as things like what block of variables, switches, and item slots is reserved for them.
My favorite tool for all things organization is Microsoft OneNote, especially for large ideas or team projects. But a plain text document can be plenty for small, simple, solo projects.
